onboarding.title: Welcome, Gatekeeper
onboarding.stepPacket: I'm Snipp, your fellow gatekeeper. This is a packet: it enters through an interface (port1), has a source, a destination and a service (tcp/443 = HTTPS). Your job: decide what happens to it.
onboarding.stepTable: This is the policy table. The firewall reads it TOP-DOWN — the first rule where ALL fields match wins. At the very bottom sits row 0: the implicit deny. Whatever no rule allows falls through there.
onboarding.stepAction: Our packet: a LAN client wants HTTPS to the internet. Rule 1 allows exactly that. So — what happens? Tap ACCEPT.
onboarding.stepPolicy: Correct. And WHICH rule matches? Tap its row.
onboarding.stepDescent: Watch: the packet walks the table and locks into rule 1. Every debrief works like this — the engine always shows you why.
onboarding.stepDone: That's it: read the packet, ACCEPT/DENY, tap the policy ID, understand the trace. The rest comes chapter by chapter. Good luck at the gate!
onboarding.hintRow1: Hint: it's the row whose fields ALL match the packet.

note.allDst: Matches any destination IP — but no DNAT traffic: that requires the VIP object in the policy.
note.allService: Matches any service (all protocols and ports).
note.vip: Policies match on the VIP object, not the internal IP.
note.fqdnUnresolved: FQDN object with no resolved address — matches nothing until DNS answers.

objectInfo.schedule: Mon–Fri 08:00–17:59 (wall clock). Outside of that the rule does not match.
objectInfo.nat: SNAT: the source IP is rewritten to the egress interface IP on the way out.

challenge.title: Challenge
challenge.intro: A large ruleset that grew over time — legacy, dead and duplicate rules included. Use the column filters and object browser to find the deciding rule.

policyLookup.title: Policy Lookup
policyLookup.invalid: Provide source interface, valid IPs and a port.

policyMenu.hint: Tip: right-click a policy row for actions — just like on a real firewall.

cliView.title: CLI: show firewall policy
cliView.hint: Like the real CLI, `show` omits defaults — a policy without a `set action` line is a DENY rule, no `set status` means enabled.

blitz.title: Blitz
blitz.intro: One small ruleset, 60 seconds on the clock. For each packet, decide: does it get through or not? First match wins — the matching rule flashes after every answer. Streaks earn bonus points.
blitz.question: Does this packet get through?

matchcheck.title: Match Check
matchcheck.intro: One rule, one packet, 45 seconds. Decide: does this rule match this packet? When it does not, the failing field lights up red after your answer — interfaces, addresses, service or schedule.
matchcheck.question: Does this rule match this packet?

debugFlow.title: CLI trace: diagnose debug flow
debugFlow.hint: This is what the same packet looks like in 'diagnose debug flow' on a real firewall — received packet, session, route lookup, then the policy decision.

doctor.title: Config Doctor
doctor.intro: A ruleset has exactly one real-world misconfiguration and a support ticket describing the symptom. Use the workbench tools (Policy Lookup, CLI, the rule table) to diagnose it, fix the rules, then run the diagnosis. Fewer edits = higher score.
doctor.hint: Fix the ruleset, then run the diagnosis to verify.
doctor.stillFailing: Diagnosis: {{count}} check(s) still failing — keep going.

diagnosis.nat-missing: The egress rule matched, but SNAT was off — return traffic never came back.
diagnosis.disabled: The right rule was there, just disabled — so traffic fell through to the deny.
diagnosis.order: A broad deny above the allow rule shadowed it — first match wins.
diagnosis.wrong-service: The allow rule permitted the wrong service — web traffic never matched it.
diagnosis.wrong-srcaddr: The allow rule's source didn't cover the LAN — the packets never matched.
diagnosis.wrong-dstintf: The allow rule's destination interface didn't match the route to the internet.
diagnosis.fqdn-unresolved: The destination was an FQDN object that had not resolved a single address — an empty set matches nothing. The rule was never wrong. It just had nothing to match against.

symptom.nat-missing: LAN users can reach the first page of some sites, but most just time out — as if replies never make it back.
symptom.disabled: Since the last change, nobody in the LAN can browse the web at all. There does seem to be a rule for it, though.
symptom.order: There is an allow rule for LAN web access, but it never takes effect — everything outbound gets blocked.
symptom.wrong-service: Web browsing from the LAN is dead, yet there IS an allow rule for outbound traffic. Maybe it permits the wrong thing?
symptom.wrong-srcaddr: Web works from some machines but not the LAN — as if the allow rule is scoped to the wrong source.
symptom.wrong-dstintf: The LAN can't reach the internet. The allow rule looks fine, but seems to send traffic out the wrong door.
symptom.fqdn-unresolved: The vendor portal is unreachable from the LAN. There is an allow rule, it names the right object, and the object looks perfectly reasonable.

matchLogic.title: Match logic
matchLogic.explain: All fields must match (AND). Within a field, any one entry is enough (OR).

dnat.title: Publish a Server
dnat.intro: A classic FortiGate task: port forwarding. An internal server has to be reachable from the internet. Create a Virtual IP (external → internal) and an inbound firewall policy that uses the VIP as its destination. Then test it from the internet.
dnat.task: Publish {{server}} ({{ip}}:{{port}}) to the internet at {{extIp}}:{{extPort}} (TCP). External users should reach the server through that address only.
dnat.vipIncomplete: Fill in all four VIP fields (external IP/port, mapped IP/port).
dnat.policyStep: Add an inbound policy — destination = the VIP (not the internal IP)
dnat.stillFailing: Test: {{count}} check(s) still failing — VIP set, and does a policy allow it in?
dnat.diagnosis: External traffic hits the VIP, gets DNAT-translated to the server, and the inbound policy lets it through.
dnat.concept: Concept: DNAT / Virtual IP / port forwarding

design.title: Change Request
design.intro: A change request is on your desk: a handful of requirements in plain prose, an empty ruleset, and the question of whether you can turn one into a firewall that does exactly that — and nothing beyond it. The checklist updates live while you build.
design.rule: Standing rule: anything not explicitly requested stays closed. Whatever you open beyond the request will show up in the review.
design.readyForReview: All requirements met — ready for review.
design.breach: Too much open: {{count}} unrequested connection(s) get through
design.hintClean: Works, but: {{overbroad}}× too broad, {{shadowed}}× dead rule — tighten it for 3 stars.
design.praiseClean: Review passed — tight objects, no dead rules. The auditor found nothing to be unhappy about, and took it personally.
design.praiseWorks: Approved. It does what was asked — though an auditor would have questions, and the time to ask them.

req.lanWeb: The LAN may reach the internet over HTTPS.
req.lanDns: The LAN may send DNS queries to 9.9.9.9.
req.lanDmzHttps: The LAN may reach the web server SRV_WEB01 over HTTPS.
req.guestWeb: Guest WiFi may reach the internet over HTTPS — nothing else.
req.adminDmzSsh: Only ADMIN_PC may manage SRV_WEB01 over SSH.
req.lanRdpOut: The LAN may use RDP outbound (remote support at a vendor).
req.guestToLan: Guest WiFi must NEVER reach the internal LAN.

note.a: The requester asks for swift implementation and has already told everyone it works.
note.b: Note from the department: "just open everything" was submitted as a proposal and rejected for reasons set out in the appendix. There is no appendix.
note.c: Last documented change to this firewall: unknown. The colleague who knew has been promoted.

routing.title: Routing Lab
routing.intro: Something does not reach its destination, and for once the ruleset is not to blame. The policies are correct and locked — you only get to touch the routing table. Route first, then policy: the route decides which interface the traffic leaves through, and a policy for the wrong interface never matches.
routing.rule: Watch out for the trap: as long as a default route exists, there is no such thing as "no route". 0.0.0.0/0 catches everything and sends it towards the internet, where the egress rule cheerfully allows it. The firewall says ACCEPT and the server is still never reached.
routing.badCidr: Needs a network in CIDR form, e.g. 172.16.0.0/24.
routing.rulesetLocked: Ruleset (read-only — the bug is not in here)

symptom.missing: Accounting cannot reach the web server. Accounting cannot reach a lot of things, but this time it really is the firewall.
symptom.wrong-iface: Since the maintenance window, traffic to the DMZ leaves towards the internet. The maintenance window is documented as completed successfully.
symptom.hijack: Someone added a route on Thursday. The change is undocumented, but very specific.

debrief.defaultRoute: The specific route was missing, so 0.0.0.0/0 took the traffic and the egress rule waved it through. A default route is not a safety net — it is a very confident guess.
debrief.dstintf: The route existed and pointed at the wrong interface. The policy for port2 was never even consulted, which is why the ruleset looked innocent. It was.
debrief.lpm: Longest prefix match does not care how correct your /24 is. A /25 is more specific, so the /25 wins. Specificity beats intent, every time.

mastery.title: Weak spots
mastery.noData: Not enough answers yet to say anything useful.
mastery.allSolid: Nothing stands out as weak. That either means you know it, or the sample is being polite.

review.title: Review
review.intro: Five short tasks, aimed at whatever you keep getting wrong. Accept or deny, then the engine shows you what it did and why.
review.noWeakness: Nothing measures as weak yet, so this round covers ground you have barely touched.
review.perfect: All five. Whatever was weak has stopped being weak, at least for today.
review.keepGoing: Noted. The weak spots update themselves, so this list will look different tomorrow.

lesson.implicitDeny: No rule matched, so policy 0 decided. It is in no list and always has the last word.
lesson.firstMatch: The first matching rule wins. Specificity does not enter into it.
lesson.interface: Interfaces are matched before addresses. A rule on the wrong pair never gets that far.
lesson.address: The address object decides, not the IP you had in mind. Check what the object actually contains.
lesson.service: The service must match protocol AND port. Close is not a port range.
lesson.schedule: A schedule turns a rule off outside its window. It looks enabled and is not, at this hour.
lesson.routing: Routing happens before the policy check and picks the outgoing interface. No route means the policy is never consulted.
lesson.vip: DNAT traffic only matches the VIP object. Neither all nor the internal IP will do it.
lesson.snat: SNAT rewrites the source to the egress interface. Without it the reply has nowhere to come back to.

notes.title: Field notes
notes.dupeFallback: The archive is complete. The chest holds something more tangible instead.
notes.empty: No notes yet. Chests contain them.
notes.hasOneFor: There are {{count}} field note(s) on this — still in a chest.

policy0.title: Policy 0
policy0.body: It appears in no list, has no ID you could click, and still decides most of the traffic. The log calls it “Implicit Deny”. It does not log by default — so the most common thing a firewall does is also the thing it talks about least.

routeFirst.title: Route before policy
routeFirst.body: Route lookup happens before the policy check and fixes the outgoing interface. With a default route there is no “no way there”; there is only the wrong way. The firewall says ACCEPT, the packet leaves obediently, and the server never hears about it.

vipOnly.title: The VIP or nothing
vipOnly.body: DNAT traffic matches the VIP object in the destination and nothing else. Not “all”, not the internal IP — the VIP. “all” sounds like everything and here it means everything except the one thing you need.

prednatPort.title: The outside port
prednatPort.body: A service is protocol AND destination port, checked against the packet as it arrives — so the outside port. Map 8443 to 443, set the service to HTTPS, and you have built a rule that never matches and a ticket nobody can read.

shadowing.title: Shadowing
shadowing.body: A broad rule on top covers every narrower rule below it. Syntactically the ruleset stays flawless; there is no error message for “this line is never reached”. The firewall executes what is written, not what was meant.

sessionTable.title: The session remembers
sessionTable.body: An established session is not re-evaluated because you changed the policy. You build the rule, test, nothing. Build it again, nothing again. Then you clear the session table and discover the first version was fine.

firstMatch.title: First match
firstMatch.body: Top to bottom, the first matching rule wins. The rule further down is not “more specific”, it is late. There are administrators who hunt a fault for three days and then find it in row two.

objectNotName.title: The object decides
objectNotName.body: Not the name. “SRV_WEB01” may point at a /24, at the wrong host, or at nothing at all, and the firewall will not complain in any of the three cases. Read names instead of contents and you are troubleshooting your own assumptions.

noNatNoReturn.title: Out but not back
noNatNoReturn.body: Without NAT the packet leaves carrying its private source address. It even arrives. It does not find its way back, and you only notice by the timestamps: requests without replies, neatly stacked.

debugFlow.title: The flow trace
debugFlow.body: There is exactly one tool that does not guess: the trace shows which rule matched and why. It is also the fastest way to be proven wrong about your own configuration, which is why it gets used less than it should.

intrazone.title: Inside the zone
intrazone.body: Traffic between interfaces of the same zone is dropped by default. Two ports, one zone, the same cosy sense of belonging — and nothing gets through until intra-zone is explicitly allowed. The fault then gets looked for in the switch.

anyAnyAll.title: any / all / ALL
anyAnyAll.body: “any” on the interfaces, “all” on the addresses, “ALL” on the service: a rule that permits everything while looking like a rule. It sits in more production systems than anyone would admit, and always just for testing.

fqdnMoves.title: FQDN
fqdnMoves.body: An FQDN object contains whatever DNS currently says. Change the record and the rule changes with nobody touching it. That is a feature. In an audit it is an explanation.

midnightSchedule.title: Across midnight
midnightSchedule.body: A window that runs across midnight needs two entries. This gets forgotten exactly once, at night, when nobody is around who could look it up.

interfaceAny.title: srcintf: any
interfaceAny.body: An interface pair sorts rules into groups a person can hold in their head. Set srcintf to “any” and that order collapses; everything stands in one long line again. Convenient in the short term. The colleague who inherits the ruleset in two years will have their own words for it.

zoneTradeoff.title: Zones
zoneTradeoff.body: Group interfaces into a zone and they vanish as individual targets — rules address the zone only. The tidiness is real. The bill arrives on the day exactly one interface needs an exception.

hitCountZero.title: Hit count zero
hitCountZero.body: A rule with no hits does nothing. It may be shadowed, disabled, or written for traffic that never existed. All three look the same in the table and get treated the same: not at all.

policyIdNotOrder.title: An ID is not a position
policyIdNotOrder.body: Move a rule and its ID stays. Sort by ID and you see an order the firewall does not use. Two numbers that look like one.

disabledRule.title: Disabled
disabledRule.body: A disabled rule stays in the table and gets skipped during matching. It looks like documentation and works as decoration. By year three nobody remembers whether it is still disabled or already.

addressGroup.title: Address groups
addressGroup.body: A group is an object containing other objects, resolved at match time. Very convenient — until someone edits one member and thereby fourteen rules at once, twelve of which they have never seen.

denyNoLog.title: Deny without log
denyNoLog.body: A deny without logging is a no that nobody hears. It works perfectly and explains nothing. When someone asks three weeks later why the application is down, the answer sits in the ruleset and not in the logs.

serviceAll.title: Service ALL
serviceAll.body: “ALL” means every protocol and every port, not “all the usual ones”. It is the fastest way to make a rule work and the most common reason it later works too well.

policyLookup.title: Policy Lookup
policyLookup.body: The lookup asks the firewall which rule a hypothetical packet would hit. It answers in four seconds what takes twenty minutes in a meeting.

scheduleLooksOn.title: Schedule
scheduleLooksOn.body: A schedule switches a rule off outside its window. The rule looks enabled the whole time. It is, too — just not now.
